title: Decision about extending a shared engine is handed back

source.note: The engine-scope choice is explicitly handed to “the primary,” and subsequent context shows a primary decision. This is an agent-to-coordinator handback, not a current request for end-user input.

messages.text: The analysis crate is recompiling against the corrected Go facts producer. The key new producer tests have already gone green; this run checks whether those facts resolve the receiver-field, range-binder, Go 1.26 conversion, and literal cases through the native engine end to end.

The analysis test binary is still compiling; concurrent analysis-crate builds are also active on the host. The selected run remains intact, and I’m letting Cargo proceed without imposing a build limit, as the lane instructions require.

Fourteen of the fifteen native point tests now pass, including the range binder, `new`, and nested literal cases. The remaining shadowed-value case exposed a shared fact-schema constraint: call records only accept callable or unsupported callee sites. I’m preserving the lexical value reference separately and marking the invocation unsupported, so the parameter resolves without emitting an invalid call fact.

The first run showed the remaining test failure was in call-fact validation, and that is corrected without weakening the resolver’s completeness reporting. The other fourteen native Go point regressions were green; I’m recompiling that suite with this correction before moving to the full trial census.

The trial failure details confirm one more true native producer gap: type-switch aliases and select receive binders have no scoped declarations, so their clause-body references are absent. I’m adding this case to the native regression suite next; the switch/select package-member checks themselves depend on the separately owned external-package context and will remain outside this lane.

The focused analysis build is taking longer because mbx evicted large incremental state, but rustc is active and has reported no new compile errors. Once this run finishes, I’ll add and exercise the clause-binder regression before changing its producer.

The latest focused build is compiling the updated native analysis crate. I’ve confirmed the compiler is still working on the analysis library, not blocked; the prior run established that literal, range, method, and `new` regressions pass, with only the call-recording issue fixed since then.

The Go 1.26 and literal fixes are confirmed end to end. The current rebuild is still active and error-free; I’m keeping the source stable until its test binary finishes, then I’ll capture the clause-binder gap with a native-only regression.

The test command is now blocked inside mbx’s shared incremental-cache registrar: one concurrent `mbx build` holds the registrar while waiting on a per-build lease, and another build holds that lease while waiting on the registrar. I’ll continue the implementation while checking the Mj coordination workflow so I can report the lock cycle to the parent without interrupting anyone else’s build.

Mj session messaging is unavailable here: the `mj` CLI cannot remove its expired log in the read-only home, and this session exposes only the final handback tool. I’ll leave the other build processes untouched and carry the lock-owner details in the handback while continuing independently.

The analysis-test caller fix is already present in this worktree as the equivalent local cherry-pick, so I’ll keep it and continue the Go resolution work. A shared mbx lock cycle has stalled test builds; I’m checking the current patch and lock state while avoiding changes to the other lane’s processes.

The lock-owning processes have exited, and the patch is formatted. I’m restarting the focused native-resolution regression now; after that I’ll run the Go and analysis suites, then the required clippy/fmt checks and final trial census.

The implementation now covers the remaining point cases with AST-derived facts: clause-local binders, typed range variables, Go 1.26 `new(expr)` and conversions, and nested named-container literals. Formatting passes. The four test runs are queued behind another workspace release build’s shared target lock; I’m leaving that build untouched and checking the regression/test evidence in parallel.

The first validation exposed two regressions in my additions. Type-switch aliases were attached to their case body even though the declaration token is in the switch guard, violating the source-range invariant; and I over-classified all visible `T(x)` syntax as a conversion, contrary to the producer’s existing ambiguous-call contract. I’m narrowing conversion handling to the Go 1.26 `new(expr)` context and attaching clause declarations to their actual AST tokens.

The clause-range panic is fixed, and the existing call-ambiguity contract is preserved. A second compile check caught a test-only slot lookup typo, which I’ve corrected; the focused Go crate and point tests are being rebuilt against that correction now.

The initial test failures are now reduced to the two source/test fixes above; the old no-trial Go test contract also exposed and helped preserve ambiguous call syntax. The corrected binaries are waiting on the shared mbx build-directory lock, so I’m using the wait to sort the prior trial census into true point failures versus the test-hook and external-package groups.

One final code audit found two new helpers that recurse through nested parentheses, which violates the repo’s stack-safe AST traversal rule. I’m converting those helpers to iterative walks and restarting the queued validations against the final source; the active test processes are mine, so I’ll stop only those runs.

The new producer test now reaches fact validation and found the remaining scope-range issue: each type-switch case binding points to the guard token, which lies before the case body’s current scope range. I’m widening those per-case scope ranges back to the guard token while keeping each binder inactive until its own case begins.

The clause scope now includes the guard token for fact validation, while each alias still activates only within its own clause; receive bindings activate after the receive statement. I’ve formatted that correction and restarted all four required Go validation runs, including the final trial census.

The clause-scope fix is in place. I’m checking the still-running trial and restarting the validation jobs that exited without producing logs, then I’ll classify its final failures and finish the required checks.

The detached jobs are being killed before Cargo records an exit status; their logs show only lock waits, so those attempts are not valid results. I’m keeping the launcher shell attached while the detached Cargo jobs finish, which preserves the lane’s required `setsid` runs and gives us reliable completion markers.

The three required Cargo suites are now attached to persistent launcher sessions. Their logs still show Cargo waiting on the shared build-directory lock, so I’m checking which job owns it while preserving all running builds.

The builds remain blocked in Cargo’s package cache and target locks, with no visible local lock owner. I’m leaving them running and checking the shared target timestamps; once the lock clears, these same sessions will proceed without another launch.

The shared target is actively compiling a Go integration-test binary, so the lock appears to belong to a live build rather than a stale lock file. Formatting already passes; I’m keeping our trial and no-trial suites queued concurrently and will take their actual results as soon as Cargo releases the target.

The requested runs are still queued behind the active shared-target build; Cargo is updating artifacts, but our run logs have not advanced past the lock messages yet. The formatting check and whitespace check pass, and I’m keeping the validations alive rather than treating these waits as test results.

The first full Go-analysis artifact has started rebuilding in the shared target, which is progress, though the nextest sessions remain queued. I also reviewed the remaining historical trial failures: the named/elided literal and nested-map-key misses are directly covered by the current producer changes and will be settled by the final run.

The earlier trial output confirms the unresolved inner receiver and package-miss assertions expect incumbent `no_definition` behavior while the native path correctly reports structured incompleteness. I’ll classify those as trial-contract artifacts; external package/context failures remain with that lane, while true producer failures such as the literal and binder cases are being fixed and rechecked.

Cargo has not released the shared build lock yet; no suite has failed, and none has produced a completion marker. I’m preserving these sessions and continuing with the source review rather than claiming a pass from an incomplete run.

The shared analysis test binary is compiling now; new `.rcgu.o` files appeared at 01:19, so the target is making progress. Our suites are still waiting for Cargo’s target lock, and I’ll let them acquire it when this compile releases it.

Cargo has moved through the analysis and language crates and produced fresh artifacts; the queued nextest sessions have not exited or reported failures. The active rebuild is large, so validation is taking longer than the earlier pre-fix runs, but the shared target is still progressing.

The focused native point suite has completed: all 19 Go point tests pass, including the new range/type-switch binders, Go 1.26 `new(expr)`, named/elided literals, and nested map keys. The full trial and no-trial package runs are still in Cargo’s queue, so I’m retaining them for the required whole-suite results.

The focused Go tests are green, and the broad trial has reached compilation of `brokk-bifrost-analysis`; that large compile has not emitted a new artifact recently. I’m watching the existing jobs and will keep the final trial ahead of reverting its temporary hook.

The current compiler has been on the analysis crate for several minutes without a fresh target artifact, but the compile has not exited and the queued tests remain active. The focused test result is already green; I’m letting this full build finish before I alter the trial hook or start the final Clippy checks.

The active trial command is still compiling the analysis crate; the run logs show no compiler error or test failure yet. The targeted native suite remains 19/19 green. Cargo’s shared build lock is the remaining bottleneck before full trial results and Clippy.

The rebuild has restarted analysis with the trial configuration and is still active; the new tests are independently green. No source change or failure has appeared since, so I’m holding the current validation queue until the broad run reports its actual count.

Fresh analysis test-binary object files are now appearing under the shared target, so the stalled-looking phase is advancing. The final trial is still the first broad run in the queue; I’m keeping the no-trial checks queued behind it.

The rebuilt analysis test executable has been produced. The full trial command is moving through compilation of its remaining dependencies; the focused 19-test result is still the only completed validation so far.

The broad trial has advanced into the Go crate and neighboring language dependencies after building the large analysis test executable. No compile errors have been reported; the final5 runner is still working through its test-profile artifacts.

I checked the lock owner without disturbing it: the first trial is in an active Mbx rustc action, while the other Cargo invocations are waiting on the same target build lock. This explains the queue and confirms it is not a test failure; I’m leaving all processes intact.

Another analysis build unit appeared in the target at 01:41, and the active Mbx compiler process is still alive. The trial has not produced results yet; the other test commands remain queued on the same Cargo target lock.

The trial build has reached the `brokk-bifrost` integration-test executables, which explains the large number of artifacts and long lock hold. It is progressing through those targets; the direct native tests still pass, and no trial failure output has appeared yet.

I found that the first detached launches continued despite initially silent logs; the focused one has passed, and the final5 trial plus no-trial suites are still queued. I’m stopping only my redundant final6 process groups so we retain one run per required suite and avoid launching duplicate nextest workloads when the build lock clears.

The full trial has entered its 1,241-test run and is reporting failures; the early ones are policy tests that depend on external Go callees and incomplete semantic context, as expected from the trial wiring. I’m letting it finish so I can classify every failure and verify the native point cases separately.

The trial finished with **1,007 passed, 234 failed, 15,943 skipped** (1,241 selected tests), versus the 996/1,230 baseline. All 19 native point tests pass, and the reported named-literal, map-key, `new(expr)`, receiver-alias, range and binder cases now produce the expected candidate or lexical binding; remaining failures in those integration fixtures report incomplete package/build-selection context or incumbent-only status expectations. The Go producer suite also passes 89/89.

The required no-trial analysis suite has passed 415/415, and the Go producer suite passed 89/89. The trial wrapper has exited with its recorded failure status. I’m removing only the two temporary trial-hook edits now, then I’ll run both Clippy modes against the final code.

The final trial log now records exit 100 from its 234 expected/integration failures, while the no-trial analysis and Go producer suites both exit 0. Formatting passes after the hook revert. The library Clippy check is compiling dependencies; the workspace Clippy job is queued behind it.

The native point fixes and trial-hook removal are complete. I’m finishing workspace Clippy, recording the per-failure trial classification, then I’ll commit the three production/test files and hand the parent the evidence.

The final trial has 234 unique failing tests. The 11 new native-point regressions all pass; the remaining failures are mainly downstream suites affected by the test-only native route, plus explicit Go package-context/provider gaps and assertions on incumbent diagnostics. The two required no-trial Go suites and analysis Go suite pass.

The library Clippy check passed, and the workspace Clippy log has completed successfully. I’m rerunning the format check to capture a clean exit status, then I’ll save a deduplicated 234-test failure ledger and commit.

The first workspace Clippy log reached Cargo’s successful `Finished` line, but its wrapper did not return an exit marker. My clean rerun hit the mbx sandbox socket restriction and fell back to FIFO transport; I’m waiting for its explicit result so the final validation is attributable.
Committed native Go point-resolution fixes as `81484c220`. Validation passed; the final trial remains at 234 failures, classified in the handback report. The worktree is clean.

I’ll revise the producer to emit only structured transfers and keep the accepted syntax/binder work and all 11 regressions. I’ll first trace the existing resolution transfer vocabulary and engine consumers, then implement only transfers the engine can consume; if one is unsupported, I’ll report that boundary instead of adding producer-side name lookup.

The producer rewrite is blocked by a real engine gap: current type transfers can only copy a resolved type identity while changing category/addressability or indirection. They cannot extract a range element/map key or a named container’s component type, and composite literal key classification still needs the selected type. I’m stopping before adding producer lookup or an unconsumed transfer kind, as directed, and handing back the exact boundary for a design decision.

I stopped before editing or committing. The current engine cannot consume the required range element/key or named composite-literal component projections; adding a transfer label alone would still copy the container’s type identity. The worktree remains clean at `81484c220`, with all 11 regressions intact.

I handed the evidence and the decision about extending the shared resolution engine to the primary.

evidence.user_prompt_tail:
binders: key/value slots from element/key transfers of the ranged expression's slot (add a transfer kind only if none fits, and say so).
- Type-switch binders: the case type's type syntax, lowered as usual; the engine binds the type name.
- `new(expr)`: decide builtin-vs-shadowed by emitting the call as an ordinary reference to `new` that the engine resolves against the universe/package scope; an unresolved or shadowed `new` stays incomplete or binds to the user declaration. Do not decide it with a same-file name set.
- Elided composite literal element types: a transfer from the enclosing literal's element type slot.
If the engine cannot yet consume one of these transfers, stop and report which one and why, instead of reintroducing producer-side lookup.

Validation as before: the 11 tests plus your focused native points scope, Go producer crate, analysis Go scope, both Clippy modes, fmt, and a trial rerun with before/after counts. Commit as a follow-up commit (do not rewrite 81484c220) and hand back the SHAs.
